metadata.title: School-level digital support and reading achievement: Evidence from the PIRLS 2021 U.S. sample

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PIRLS 2021 microdata for the United States, where the sampling design is a two-stage stratified cluster sample (schools selected with PPS, then classrooms sampled within schools). The authors report that they incorporate PIRLS-supplied sampling weights to account for the complex design and to ensure representativeness of the U.S. fifth-grade population. Because the analysis is conducted in R using multiple linear regression with plausible values, the weighting is intended to correct for unequal selection probabilities and clustering at the school/classroom levels. The manuscript does not report replicate-weight methodology (e.g., BRR/jackknife), so uncertainty estimation is described only at the level of the weighted model rather than via explicit replicate procedures.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the PIRLS 2021 U.S. national sample of fifth-grade students administered in fall 2021 due to COVID-19 disruptions. The analytic sample is described as nationally representative, drawn from 78 schools with two classrooms per selected school (with very small classrooms combined into pseudo-classrooms), and includes students assessed in those selected classrooms/pseudo-classrooms. The study does not specify additional exclusions beyond the use of multiple imputation across the five plausible values.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Multiple linear regression with plausible values (5 PVs). Teacher technological support: B = 58.37, SE = 12.12, t = 4.82, p < .001. School internet connection: B = –57.07, SE = 8.78, t = –6.50, p < .001. Pseudo-R² = .217.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2021 U.S. Grade 5 reading achievement (PVs) the study leveraged teacher technological support, school internet connection, locating-information instruction grade, and parental involvement emphasis to model reading achievement, finding that teacher technological support had a strong positive association (B = 58.37, p < .001) while school internet connection had a significant negative association (B = –57.07, p < .001). This indicates that digital equity policies should prioritize instructional guidance and teacher-mediated technology integration rather than relying on connectivity alone, while also recognizing that the study is correlational and does not establish causality.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PIRLS 2021 U.S. Grade 5 reading achievement using five plausible values (PVs) and a weighted multiple linear regression framework with multiple imputation across PVs. The analytic sample is nationally representative (1657 students from 78 schools). Results show a significant negative main effect of school internet connection on reading achievement (B = –57.07, p < .001) and a significant positive main effect of teacher technological support (B = 58.37, p < .001), with a reported pseudo-R² of .217. Moderation effects indicate that internet access is more effective when students receive early instruction in locating information within texts (Internet × Locating skill: B = 25.28, p < .001), while teacher support is less beneficial when locating instruction is delayed (Teacher support × Locating skill: B = –19.33, p < .001). The authors caution that associations are not causal and that PIRLS measures rely on principal-reported contextual information, with limited school/district granularity and a nested data structure that would ideally be handled with multilevel modeling.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This paper is an empirical regression-based study using PIRLS 2021 plausible values and sampling weights, but it does not train or evaluate any machine learning predictive models (no ML algorithms are reported in the Methods/Results). Therefore, the ML technique fields are left empty and the extraction focuses on the regression findings and their moderated relationships. The study’s design is best classified as exploratory because it tests associations and interactions rather than performing predictive ML model comparison.
